1:
Gill opens by dividing the subject, since the Israelites waged two sorts of war which Maimonides distinguishes: one commanded, as against the seven nations of Canaan, and one permitted and voluntary, left to their own discretion when they were provoked or invaded, in which they might act the offensive or the defensive part or both. Keil and Delitzsch read the whole chapter as governing the second kind, wars against nations outside Canaan, and state its purpose as a single humane principle, that the people of God were to spare as much as possible the lives of their own soldiers and of their enemies alike — hence the exemptions, the offer of peace, the sparing of women and children, and the protection of the fruit-trees. Ellicott makes the same point from the opening phrase, which is general and not confined to the immediate conquest, and observes that Moses foresees a gradual completion in which Israel must go to battle many times. He adds a military note, that the Israelite army was composed chiefly or entirely of infantry in most of its great victories, which is why the sight of horses and chariots needed to be met with a command not to fear.

Calvin classes the law under the first commandment rather than under the civil code, since its point is that Israel should carry on its wars under the auspices of God and rest its hope of safety on nothing but the invocation of his name; from which he draws the general rule that the worship of God is by no means to be passed over in civil and earthly government, for though such government aims directly at preserving equity between men, religion always ought to hold the first place. Amid the very clang of arms, he says, they were not to fall into such confusion as to forget whose guardianship they were under. Henry finds the tone of the whole code remarkable in a different way, that the discipline of war prescribed here has nothing of the harshness usual in martial law, the intent being throughout to encourage the soldiers and make their service easy. He sets out the two grounds of encouragement they were to carry: the presence of God with them, and the experience they and their fathers had of his power in bringing them out of Egypt, since he who saved them from greater enemies would not let them be run down by lesser ones.

On the speaker Keil and Delitzsch are precise: not the high priest but the priest who accompanied the army, as Phinehas did against Midian, whom the Rabbins style the anointed of the battle and raise to the highest dignity next to the high priest, though on no better ground than that one passage. Henry knows the same title and turns it to account, calling it a proper name for the captain of our salvation, and asking who is fitter to encourage the people than the man whose office it is to pray for them. Clarke widens the frame to comparative practice, that almost all ancient nations took their priests to battle, since they did not expect success without the object of their adoration present and supposed they secured it by bringing his representative. Ellicott draws a limit from the same fact, that since the priest's words are in effect the blessing of Jehovah on the campaign, Israel could not lawfully go to war except where that blessing might be invoked. Calvin counts the four expressions forbidding fear and takes the heaping of them as a measure of how hard that evil is to cure. Gill notes the address was spoken in Hebrew.
5:
Calvin files the exemptions under the prohibition of theft, which sounds remote until he states the reasoning: if it is hard that a man should be deprived by war of the use of his new house or the produce of his vineyard, how much harsher to strip men of their fortunes or drive them from lands they justly call their own. He adds the civil argument, that since the state needs houses built and vineyards planted, and men will not address themselves to such work with alacrity unless encouraged by the hope of enjoying it, God grants this indulgence. Clarke explains what dedicating a house meant, citing the title of a psalm as evidence that Israel dedicated new houses with prayer and thanksgiving to secure the divine presence, since no pious man could imagine dwelling safely in a house not under God's protection; and he notes that even barbarous nations consecrate part of a new house to their deity, instancing houses on the African coast with one of three rooms given to the serpent god. Gill confesses he cannot say certainly what the officers were, since they are distinguished from the captains and the word elsewhere describes those who attended the judges.

The vineyard clause turns on a technical word. Gill and Wesley both read the Hebrew as not having made it common, and both explain it from the law of the fruit of trees: three years the fruit might not be eaten, in the fourth it was devoted to the Lord and could be redeemed from the priest and so made common, and only in the fifth was it eaten in course. Gill reports a rival derivation from Aben Ezra, who traces the word instead to piping and dancing, on the ground that it was a custom to sing and dance in vineyards. Wesley adds the reason of state, that these dispensations were generally convenient but especially necessary at the beginning of the settlement, to encourage men to work that was costly to themselves and useful to the commonwealth. Clarke supplies the marriage custom behind the third exemption, that the parties were contracted and then left in their parents' houses until the bridegroom had made his preparations, so that to be called away at that moment was reckoned an excessive hardship; and he reaches for Homer, whose Protesilaus went to Troy leaving his wife in the deepest distress and his house unfinished.

Wesley limits every one of these releases to a war that God allowed rather than commanded, noting that in the approaching Canaanite war not even the bridegroom was exempted. On the last exemption Clarke observes that the word for fearful means tender or soft-hearted, and that soft indeed must the heart be which after such a public permission could still turn its back on enemies and brethren; he finds the case tried in Gideon, where the same offer left ten thousand of thirty-two thousand standing, so that no deception was possible and the departure of the rest was the fullest proof of their cowardice. Keil and Delitzsch give the reason from the Hebrew, that the brethren's heart may not flow away. On the closing verse they hold that the same officers who raised and organised the men were to appoint captains over them, rejecting the rendering that would make it a matter of leading the command. Wesley reads it the other way, that the Hebrew means the captains were to be set at the head of the people under their charge, since it is not likely they had their captains still to make when the battle was upon them. Ellicott takes them for leaders of the campaign only.
10:
Henry treats the summons as a rule of honour before it is a rule of war: Israel was not to descend on any neighbour without first giving fair notice by a public statement of the ground of the quarrel, since in dealing with the worst of enemies the laws of justice must be observed, and as the sword is never to be taken in hand without cause, so not without cause shown — war being an appeal in which the merits must be set forth. To the proclamation itself a tender of peace was to be joined, on terms which the Jewish writers make include the renouncing of idolatry. Calvin states the same principle as a restraint: even in lawful wars cruelty is to be repressed and bloodshed avoided as far as possible, the inhabitants being first exhorted to capitulate and, if they do, kept alive under tribute; and he observes that this equity was naturally implanted in all nations, which is how heralds arose in the first place. Clarke notes that interpreters are greatly divided about which cities the law covers, and holds that the context restricts the offer to towns outside the seven devoted nations.

Keil and Delitzsch set out the two outcomes plainly: a town that opened its gates became tributary and served, while a town that chose war was to be besieged, its males put to the sword and its spoil left to the besiegers for their own maintenance. Calvin will not pass that second clause without protest, and the protest is the strongest thing in the chapter. The permission seems to confer too great a licence, he says, since even heathen writers command the conquered to be spared and require that men be admitted to mercy who lay down their arms and throw themselves on the good faith of the general, though the battering-ram have already breached the wall — so how does God, the Father of mercies, give his sanction to indiscriminate bloodshed? His answer does not defend the letter but concedes it: more was allowed the Jews on account of their hardness of heart than was justly lawful for them, since by the law of charity even armed men should be spared if they cast away the sword and crave mercy. Gill, working the other side of the case, notes that the offer belongs to a war of their own choosing.

Gill gives a reason for each class that is spared, and the reasons are not identical: the women for the weakness of their sex and their subjection to their husbands, the little ones, males as well as females, for their tender age, and the cattle for their insensibility — the common thread being that none of them had any part in holding out the siege. On the phrase about cities very far off he draws the boundary at the land of Israel, so that the neighbouring nations are meant, since Israel never made war on distant peoples unless invaded and never carried its conquests far even under its most powerful kings. Calvin explains why the Canaanites stand outside these rules altogether: God had not merely armed the Jews against them but appointed them the ministers and executioners of his vengeance, having borne with those nations four hundred years while they grew steadily worse in their obstinacy, so that their desperate impiety was manifest; and since the land itself was consecrated to God's service, inhabitants who could do nothing but contaminate it had to be removed. Keil and Delitzsch note that the word for every breath is to be understood of human beings only.
16:
The exception for the seven nations is where the commentators become least comfortable, and Clarke tries to soften it by translation. He suggests the Hebrew may be rendered thou shalt utterly subdue them, slaying those who resist, or else expelling them from the land or reducing them to servitude in it, so that what is decreed is the end of their political existence as a people rather than the killing of every person. He finds a test case in the Gibeonites, who evidently understood that they must either be slain or leave, since the second was in their power and they resorted to a stratagem instead; and when the deceit came out, Israel, though not bound by an oath obtained by fraud and with this very command before their eyes, did not think itself obliged to put the deceivers to death, but ended their political existence by making them hewers of wood and drawers of water. Gill reports a related opinion, that Joshua proclaimed peace to all the cities of Canaan and destroyed only those that refused, the Gibeonites having supposedly not heard of it; and he notes with Jarchi that any who repented and became proselytes might be received.

Gill returns to the same point on the following verse, where the stated reason is not the guilt of the nations but the danger of contagion, that they teach you not to do after all their abominations; and he observes that this is exactly why proselytes could be suffered to live among Israel, since from them no such danger came, even the proselytes of the gate having renounced idolatry. Keil and Delitzsch keep the terms strict, taking the ban to mean these nations were to be altogether exterminated so that they might not teach Israel their abominations and sins, and confining the phrase about every breath to human beings rather than to all that lives. Wesley makes the same restriction in a line, that nothing means no man, since the beasts with few exceptions were given to Israel for a prey. The disagreement is therefore narrower than it first appears: all of them read the clause about teaching as the reason of the law, and they divide over whether the sentence it grounds is the destruction of persons or the destruction of a people.

Clarke presses his reading with evidence from later history, and it is the strongest part of his case. Rahab and her household were spared, so it does not appear that Israel believed itself bound to put every Canaanite to death; and that many of them remained in the land as late as Solomon is beyond dispute, since the record says expressly that all the people left of the Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites, whom the children of Israel had not consumed, were made by Solomon to pay tribute. Solomon, on this showing, destroyed their political existence without considering himself bound by the law to destroy their lives. Gill reaches a similar result from a different direction, observing that many were in fact suffered to live among Israel, which he supposes was allowed on their becoming proselytes, that being one of the terms of peace, as with Rahab and her household. Both therefore end where Jarchi does, that repentance and proselytism were a way out of the sentence, though neither pretends that the text says so.
19:
Calvin attaches the law about trees to the commandment against theft, and gives the inference that follows: if God restrains the liberty of inflicting injury in the very heat of war, much more did he mean his people to abstain from mischief in time of peace. Though the laws of war opened the gate to plunder, they were to take care that the land should not be left barren for the future, so that booty was to be taken with the advantage of the human race still in view and posterity still nourished by trees that do not quickly come to bearing. He gives two reasons for sparing fruit-trees in particular, first that they supply food to all men and so manifest the blessing of God, and second that trees are exposed to everybody and defenceless, by which he understands the text to mean that war is not to be waged with them as with men. Wesley narrows the prohibition to a general destruction rather than the cutting of a few as the convenience of the siege required, and glosses the difficult phrase about man's life as meaning the sustenance or support of his life.

Clarke calls the original exceedingly obscure and lays out four renderings side by side without choosing: that the trees of the field are for a man to employ in the siege; that it is man and the tree of the field that must go before him for a bulwark; that it is a tree and not men, to increase the number of those who come against him; and that the tree of the field is as a man, to go before his face for a bulwark. He judges that the sense is clear enough even where the strict grammatical meaning cannot be settled, since the provision was merciful in sparing what yielded the fruit that supported life, and was sound policy besides, because even conquerors must perish if the means of life are cut off; it is diabolic cruelty, he adds, to add the horrors of famine to the miseries of war. Calvin acknowledges the same variety of explanations. Gill collects the rabbinic reckoning of the phrase about many days, where days signify two and many three, and reports the rule drawn from it that a siege is not begun less than three days before the sabbath.

On the permission that follows, Keil and Delitzsch render the clause closely: only trees known not to bear edible fruit may be hewn down, and with them a rampart built against the town until it come down, the verb being the one used elsewhere of lofty fortifications falling or sinking from their eminence. They trace the noun for siege to a root meaning to compress or force down, so that to come into siege is to be hemmed in, and note that the same word does duty for the means of hemming in, the besieging rampart itself. Gill describes the uses more concretely, the felled timber serving to raise batteries or to make engines for casting stones into the city and so pressing the inhabitants to surrender, and observes that the barren trees might be known as such by other tokens than fruit, since a siege might fall in a season when no tree bore any. He closes by reading the whole provision as an emblem, the axe laid to fruitless trees in a moral sense while trees of righteousness, the planting of the Lord, are preserved and never rooted up.
